ca_left_of_peapod.blurb: A stretch of the volcanic rock band on Eagle Peak, high above the Lassen Peak trailhead at roughly 8,700 feet. Mostly bolted lines with a handful of trad and top-rope options, and the grades lean harder than the neighboring sections: expect plenty of 5.10 and 5.11 with a few 5.12s and some projects. Because most climbers settle on the easier side of the formation, this end tends to be quieter. Several bolts are old and the rock can be loose in places, so treat it with some care, and climb it dry. The walk-up is a bit over half an hour, and early-season snow can linger on the approach. Peon U is the one named test-piece here.
ca_left_of_peapod.parking_note: Leave the car in the Lassen Peak trailhead lot on the park road; the walk to the rock begins from there.
ca_left_of_peapod.approach: From the Lassen Peak lot, take the main trail briefly, then fork left onto a narrow path around the base of the hill. Cross the open flat toward Eagle Peak and climb the steep slope to the rock band, then continue a few minutes along its base to reach this section. Snow can hide the cairned path for a long time.

ca_right_wall.blurb: The first big section of cliff you reach at the base of the backcountry granite on Eagle Peak in the San Diego mountains. This is steep sport climbing, mostly bolted lines in the 5.10 to 5.12 range with a few trad routes mixed in. Several of the best are Soy Chango, Up Stream, Power Pod, Fly Away Roof, Crazy Horse and White Arete. Summer heat is serious at the base, but the steep face drops into shade in the afternoon, which makes a late start workable on warm days; cooler months are far more comfortable. Allow a real hike in, and expect a scramble over grassy ledges to reach the far-right lines.
ca_right_wall.parking_note: Follow the graded dirt of Boulder Creek Road past the end of the pavement to a gated trailhead at a hairpin bend. The lot is on a slope, so level it if you plan to sleep in a vehicle.

ca_cold_springs_dome.blurb: A small, out-of-the-way dome in the Gibraltar area above Santa Barbara, known for good climbing packed into a modest number of lines and for staying shady in summer. Sport and trad routes sit side by side, from 5.7 up to the low 5.12s, with the bulk of the climbing between 5.10 and 5.12; a few longer sport lines run two or three pitches. Makunaima is the trad test-piece, and other favorites include Homo Slopiens, Predators Keep the Balance and Laughing Lily. Expect a steep, loose-feeling trail down to the base, and a quiet day compared with the main Santa Barbara crags.
ca_cold_springs_dome.parking_note: Drive up Gibraltar Road and leave the car at the Gibraltar Rock turnoff; the hike starts from there.
ca_cold_springs_dome.approach: Climb the ridge past the Hole-in-the-Rock boulder, then take the small climbers' path on the right and descend a steep, slippery trail to the base. Most routes lie along the base to the left.

ca_toe_the.blurb: A south-facing granite buttress on El Cajon Mountain east of San Diego, and the friendliest corner of the Mountaineer Walls. The routes here run from easy 5th class through 5.12, with an unusually large share of moderates in the 5.7 to 5.10 range, plus a mix of sport and trad lines. It suits winter days best, when the sun feels good and the breeze keeps the stone comfortable. Call Her Daddy, Chimney Fire Drill, COVID and I Love Red are the lines people single out. The approach is a short trail walk from the road.
ca_toe_the.parking_note: Pull off on the north side of El Monte Road, roughly 5.6 miles east of Lake Jennings Road, near the tall utility poles; the trail starts a few hundred feet east.
ca_toe_the.approach: Cross the footbridge over the river and follow the Mountaineers Wall trail, taking the first fork marked for The Toe and then the downhill left branch. An alternative is the dirt road past the quarry, turning right at the Toe sign.

ca_cracked_wall.blurb: The most popular wall on Bishop Peak, a volcanic plug rising above San Luis Obispo, where the stone is finely featured and often slabby. A mix of trad, sport and top-rope lines, mostly 5.9 to 5.11 with a few easier and harder ones, and many routes carry fixed anchors. Camel, Only Way To Fly, Western Airlines, Civilized Evil and Llama are among the favorites. Sunny weekends bring crowds, and shaded sections can stay mossy or damp early in the day. The walk from town is short on a well-marked trail.
ca_cracked_wall.parking_note: Take Highland Drive west from Santa Rosa Street to its end at a cul-de-sac and park on the street; this is a residential neighborhood, so keep noise down.
ca_cracked_wall.approach: A signed trail leaves the cul-de-sac and heads up through oaks to the wall; it is a short walk.

ca_1_west_wall.blurb: The far-west end of Pigeon Cliff, a roadside crag at the edge of Susanville. Mostly crack and corner climbing protected with gear, with a few bolted lines and top-rope options. This is the part of the cliff with the most easy and moderate routes, and the grades cluster around 5.9 to 5.10 with a handful of harder ones up to 5.13. Sack Lunge, Dirty Bird, I Thought This Was No Hands, Jazz Hands and Pariah are the named favorites. The base can be steep and overgrown, and the cliff stays in shade until around midday in summer; sunny winter days are pleasant. Bring a standard rack with doubles in the finger to off-hand sizes.
ca_1_west_wall.parking_note: Use the long pullout along the cliff edge on Highway 36 on the west side of town, close to where North Pine Drive meets the highway.
ca_1_west_wall.approach: Essentially none: the routes are right beside the road. Walk to the western end of the cliff, just past the River View Crack.

ca_main_wall_11.blurb: The central stretch of the big granite face at Lover's Leap above Highway 50, with walls up to roughly 600 feet. Long, mostly trad lines follow cracks and corners, with horizontal dikes giving rests and holds. Grades cluster from 5.9 to 5.11, with a few easier and a few harder, and a handful of bolted lines sit on the Tombstone Buttress. Corrugation Corner and Traveler Buttress are the classic moderates; Tombstone Terror, Freak Show, Power Lust and Boot Hill stretch the grade. The hike in is under half an hour on a wide, maintained trail, and the cliff draws visitors from across the country, so expect company on good weekends.
ca_main_wall_11.parking_note: Turn off Highway 50 onto Strawberry Lane just past the lodge and park in the lot at its end; the trail leaves from the back of the lot.
ca_main_wall_11.approach: Follow the wide, well-kept trail from the back of the lot up to the base of the cliff; the Main Wall is the second section from the west, past the West Wall.

ca_kernville_rock_a_k_a_kern_slabs.blurb: A big granite slab perched above the Kern River north of Kernville. Face and crack climbing on moderate, low-angle rock, with sport and trad lines mixed together; most routes fall between 5.7 and 5.10, with a few harder. The Lieback and Chouinard Special are the old-school trad favorites, while Friction Brewing, IP Yay! and Old Dog, New Tricks are good bolted options. A few older lines are bold or runout. Late fall through late spring is the pleasant window, since summer sun is fierce; rattlesnakes are around in spring, especially near the base. The trail up is short but steep.
ca_kernville_rock_a_k_a_kern_slabs.parking_note: Drive about five miles north from Kernville on the river road and park in the large pullout on the right, across from the Thunderbird day-use area.
ca_kernville_rock_a_k_a_kern_slabs.approach: A steep trail climbs from the back of the pullout up to the dome; at the top go left for the lower bolted wall or up and right for the classic routes.

ca_kirkwood_lake.blurb: A cluster of high-elevation boulders near Kirkwood Lake off Carson Pass, at around 7,700 feet among pines. Bouldering only, with problems roughly 10 to 20 feet tall, and the grades run hard: much of what is here is V7 and up, with V10 the most common grade and only a few easier lines. Ashy to Classy, Ill Cave, Demon On A Leash, Dabbers Roof and Black Licorice Overdose are the ones people talk about. Mornings are coolest, afternoon storms can build quickly, and trails between boulders are faint, so carry an offline map.
ca_kirkwood_lake.parking_note: Turn onto Kirkwood Lake Road from Highway 88 near Kirkwood and use the roadside turnouts; most boulders lie on the east side of the road.
